16 October 2026

$18 million price tag sees ACT ditch electronic monitoring despite big jump in family violence

15 October 2026 | By Naziya Alvi Rahman
Join the conversation
19

The ACT Government has shelved its plans to implement electronic monitoring of violent perpetrators in the Territory citing cost pressures. Photo: yasharu.

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:24
Instaread

The ACT Government has abandoned its 2024 election commitment to introduce electronic monitoring of offenders, citing an annual cost of up to $18 million, despite domestic and family violence incidents rising 33 per cent over five years.

The decision has sparked a furious response from women’s safety advocates, who accuse the government of putting budget pressures ahead of protecting victim-survivors.

The ACT remains the only Australian jurisdiction without electronic monitoring technology, commonly used through GPS-enabled ankle bracelets to track offenders in the community.

YWCA Canberra chief executive officer Frances Crimmins said the decision sent a devastating message to women experiencing violence.

“The ACT Government has put a price on women’s safety,” her organisation said in a statement.

The government’s decision comes as ACT Policing’s latest annual report reveals officers attended 4478 domestic and family violence incidents, with reported incidents increasing by 33 per cent over the past five years.

The government had promised a staged rollout of electronic monitoring, beginning with offenders on intensive correction orders, parole, limited bail and leave permits.

Later stages were expected to include home detention, early release, post-release supervision, and intensive monitoring of domestic and family violence perpetrators.

But after years of feasibility studies and consultation, the government has now ruled out implementation during the current term.

A Justice and Community Safety Directorate spokesperson said the proposed system would be expensive to establish and operate.

The feasibility study estimated annual base costs of more than $4 million to monitor a relatively small number of offenders under community corrections supervision, rising to more than $18 million for a domestic and family violence monitoring scheme. These figures exclude initial establishment costs.

READ ALSO ACT public schools face another week of disruptions as teachers demand staffing guarantees

The spokesperson said effective monitoring, particularly for domestic violence perpetrators, required more than simply fitting offenders with ankle bracelets.

It would need comprehensive risk assessments, responsive monitoring systems, effective supervision, information-sharing between agencies and safety planning with people at risk of further harm.

While acknowledging electronic monitoring could improve compliance with community-based orders and promote public safety, the government said competing financial priorities meant the scheme could not proceed.

Treasurer Chris Steel defended the decision, saying the government had to weigh the scheme against other spending commitments.

“It’s not a matter directly in my portfolio responsibilities, but I’ll say generally as the Treasurer that when we’re looking at the range of priorities in the budget, we do have to make sure that our decisions are affordable,” he said.

“Spending $18 million on that in the short-term wasn’t going to be a priority when there are a huge range of other priorities both in corrections and right across government.”

Mr Steel compared the annual cost to an additional 1 per cent increase in territory rates, above existing increases.

Asked whether abandoning the 2024 commitment raised questions about other election promises, he maintained the government was continuing to deliver its broader agenda.

READ ALSO Here's an idea from left field: make the ACT a low-tax honeypot

He pointed to commitments including the new Canberra aquatic facility and investment in social infrastructure.

“That one didn’t stack up and so we weren’t going to move forward with a project that was going to cost $18 million in the short-term,” he said.

The government had allocated $377,000 over two years in its 2023–24 Budget to investigate and develop an implementation plan.

In 2024, it indicated the scheme could be introduced within months, but no implementation funding was included in the 2025–26 Budget.

Instead, remaining funds were directed towards feasibility studies and policy work.

During budget estimates, Justice and Community Safety Directorate director-general Ray Johnson acknowledged that no priority group had been selected.

“They all carry a different level of risk … there might be a greater value but [also] a greater risk in different cohorts and there might be an order of batting … on where you start,” he told the hearing.

For women’s safety advocates, the latest decision raises questions about why the government continued consulting on the scheme without ultimately committing to its introduction.

YWCA Canberra said it had participated in consultations on the proposed monitoring system in good faith, providing advice on its design and operation.

The organisation said it had warned at the time that the ACT was already well behind other jurisdictions.

Ms Crimmins criticised the government’s lack of transparency, saying it had consulted extensively with the women’s safety sector on the design and implementation of electronic monitoring, only to quietly abandon the scheme.

She said the decision was buried in a 12 June Legislative Assembly speech, with the government citing significant cost pressures and competing priorities.

YWCA Canberra said the decision was especially disappointing given the ACT Government’s participation in National Cabinet commitments to strengthen perpetrator accountability and work towards ending violence against women and children within a generation.

The organisation accused the government of prioritising financial considerations and offender outcomes over women’s safety.

ACT Greens justice spokesperson Rebecca Vassarotti, who advocated for electronic monitoring in the Legislative Assembly, criticised the decision, saying the government needed to accept that effective justice reforms cost money.

“Electronic monitoring is a humane and compassionate alternative that protects our community while giving past offenders a genuine chance at a fresh start,” she said.

Ms Vassarotti argued that longer prison sentences could undermine rehabilitation and questioned how the government planned to address rising costs and capacity pressures at the Alexander Maconochie Centre.

She accused the government of prioritising “cuts and austerity” over practical solutions.

Tom McLuckie6:54 am 16 Oct 26

Email Part 2 31 March 2025. Amendments to legislation are required to establish how EM can be imposed, the obligations of corrections officers in supervising EM orders, and the information-sharing framework. Human rights and privacy considerations will also be addressed. While the legislative framework will define EM’s application, decisions on its use will ultimately be made by the Courts and the Sentence Administration Board based on prior offending behaviour. It is likely that any legislation introduced in the Assembly would be the subject of an Assembly committee inquiry.

Before the 2024 election, the government committed to trialling EM for domestic and family violence perpetrators, aligning with discussions at the May 2024 National Cabinet meeting on gender-based violence. To build confidence in the ACT system, a staged approach is being developed, with the first phase focused on existing community-based orders. The government is currently engaging with stakeholders to explore implementation options.

Public safety remains a priority, and the government recognises the community’s concerns about recidivist offenders and the impact of crime. Building public and operational confidence in the implementation of EM is very important, so developing a robust legal and operational framework that is supported by key stakeholders is a key to the success of the scheme.

I appreciate your engagement on this issue and will provide further updates as the project progresses.

Kind regards, Marisa.
NO FURTHER UPDATES WERE EVER PROVIDED.

Reply
Tom McLuckie6:52 am 16 Oct 26

Email Part 1 31 March 2025. From: PATERSON
Date: Mon, Mar 31, 2025 at 12:43 PM
Subject: FW: Update requested regarding the electronic tagging pilot
Dear Tom,
Thank you for your inquiry regarding the ACT Government’s progress on the electronic monitoring (EM) pilot program.
The government remains committed to implementing EM as a tool to improve compliance with community-based orders. However, as seen in other jurisdictions, EM is a tool to identify non-compliance with location based orders.
Key updates on the EM project:
The government is still in the planning phase, and implementation will require amendments to legislation, budget allocation, and procurement of EM devices and ICT systems. Initial feasibility work was funded through the 2023-24 Budget, with additional funding from the Confiscated Assets Trust Fund supporting the EM Project Manager role for 12 months.
Further the recent Budget Review provides $259,000 in 2024-25 to continue planning and consultation to inform the introduction of electronic monitoring for offenders in the ACT. The funding provides for staffing to continue work on developing the policy and legislative framework; to design a monitoring and response model and to undertake the planning required to engage a supplier to provide an electronic monitoring system. Work will also be undertaken to ensure operational agencies are in a position to implement electronic monitoring as soon as possible. This work will inform what is anticipated to be a staged implementation of electronic monitoring, including consideration of the most appropriate approach and timeframe for delivery of the Government’s commitment to trial electronic monitoring for domestic and family violence offenders. This will give victim survivors, the domestic and family violence sector and the broader community confidence that the electronic monitoring system is safe for use.

Reply
Tom McLuckie6:44 am 16 Oct 26

This was one of the recommendations from the Dangerous Driving Inquiry held in 2022. The Paper was published on 20 April 2023.
Recommendation 18: The Committee recommends that the ACT Government provide a status update on their scoping and feasibility work on electronic monitoring options to the Assembly and include consideration of using electronic monitoring to observe and check speeding drivers, with an update on progress to be tabled in the Assembly at the same time as the government response to this report.
The Government responded August 2023.
Agreed. The ACT Government has undertaken preliminary work to inform the development of a feasibility and scoping project for adopting electronic monitoring in the ACT, including research and discussions with other Australian jurisdictions, discussions with key ACT Government stakeholders and desk-based research on the technical capabilities and practical application of electronic monitoring. This is informing detailed project planning underway for the feasibility and scoping project which will consider the identification of suitable points in the justice system to adopt electronic monitoring, costs and operational implementation including data governance and system security. Consideration is also being given to developing a small-scale trial of electronic monitoring to support the feasibility and scoping project to provide a better understanding of the complexities of a larger scale introduction should this prove viable for the ACT. The ACT Government has committed $377,000 over two years in the 2023-2024 budget to undertake the feasibility and scoping work.
Andrew Barr in May 2024 then claimed the implementation was a matter of months away. In my next post, I’ll share the update I received from Minister Paterson from 31 March 2025.
